literal:
Literal Interpretation

Abram's Return from Egypt

Genesis 13 opens with Abram returning from Egypt to the Negev, accompanied by his wife Sarai and his nephew Lot, along with all their possessions. The text emphasizes that "Abram was very rich in cattle, and in silver, and in gold" (Gen 13:2). This wealth, acquired during their sojourn in Egypt, would soon become a source of tension between the two households.

Abram's journey takes him back to the place between Bethel and Hai, "where he had before pitched his tent" (Gen 13:3) and where he had previously built an altar. This return to the place of worship marks a spiritual restoration after the Egyptian sojourn. St. Augustine notes in his City of God that this return signified Abram's renewed fellowship with God after a period of testing.

The Strife Between the Herdsmen

The prosperity of both Abram and Lot created practical difficulties: "The land was not able to bear them, that they might dwell together: for their substance was great, and they could not dwell together" (Gen 13:6). Strife arose between the herdsmen of Abram and those of Lot over pasturage and water rights.

The sacred writer adds a significant detail: "And the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled at that time in the land" (Gen 13:7). This notation reminds readers that the conflict occurred under the watchful eyes of pagan peoples. The conduct of Abram and Lot in resolving their dispute would serve as a testimony to these neighboring nations.

St. Augustine, in City of God Book XVI, Chapter 20, observes that this strife arose from material abundance rather than moral failing:

"On Abraham's return out of Egypt to the place he had left, Lot, his brother's son, departed from him into the land of Sodom, without breach of charity. For they had grown rich, and began to have many herdmen of cattle, and when these strove together, they avoided in this way the pugnacious discord of their families."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 20

Abram's Generous Proposal

Abram, though the elder and the one to whom God had promised the land, took the initiative in resolving the conflict. He addressed Lot with remarkable magnanimity: "Let there be no strife, I beseech thee, between me and thee, and between my herdsmen and thy herdsmen: for we are brethren" (Gen 13:8). He then offered Lot first choice of the land, a gesture of extraordinary generosity given Abram's position as patriarch and recipient of the divine promise.

Augustine comments on the significance of this gesture:

"From this, perhaps, has arisen a pacific custom among men, that when there is any partition of earthly things, the greater should make the division, the less the choice."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 20

Lot's Choice of Sodom

When given the choice, Lot "lifted up his eyes, and saw all the country about the Jordan, which was watered throughout" (Gen 13:10). The text describes this region as being "as the paradise of the Lord, and like Egypt" before the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. The comparison to Eden and to fertile Egypt indicates the exceptional agricultural value of the Jordan plain.

Lot chose based on what appeared advantageous to natural sight: "Lot chose to himself the country about the Jordan, and he departed from the east" (Gen 13:11). He pitched his tent "even to Sodom," a city whose inhabitants "were very wicked, and sinners before the face of the Lord beyond measure" (Gen 13:12-13). The ominous foreshadowing in these verses prepares readers for the catastrophe to come in Genesis 19.

God's Renewed Promise to Abram

After Lot's departure, God spoke again to Abram, renewing and expanding His promises. The Lord commanded Abram to survey the land in all directions: "Lift up thy eyes, and look from the place wherein thou now standest, to the north and to the south, to the east and to the west" (Gen 13:14). God promised to give all this land to Abram and his seed forever.

The promise includes a striking image of abundance: "I will make thy seed as the dust of the earth: if any man be able to number the dust of the earth, he shall be able to number thy seed also" (Gen 13:16). Augustine addresses this hyperbolic language in his commentary:

"The clause 'And I will make your seed as the dust of the earth' may refer to this, being spoken by that figure the Greeks call hyperbole, which is figurative, not literal. No person of understanding can doubt how Scripture uses this and other figures."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 21

Augustine further explains that this promise encompasses more than Abram's physical descendants:

"For who does not see how incomparably larger the number of the dust must be than all men from Adam to the end of the world? How much greater must it be than the seed of Abraham--not only that pertaining to the nation of Israel, but also that which is and shall be according to the imitation of faith in all nations of the whole wide world!"

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 21

Abram's Settlement at Mamre

The chapter concludes with Abram moving his tent to dwell "by the vale of Mamre, which is in Hebron" (Gen 13:18), where he built another altar to the Lord. The name Mamre means "vision," and Hebron means "communion" or "fellowship"--fitting names for the place where Abram would receive further divine revelations and enjoy continued fellowship with God. This altar-building demonstrates Abram's habitual practice of worship, marking each significant location in his journey with an act of devotion to the Lord.
allegorical:
Allegorical Interpretation

Abram as Type of Christ and the Faithful Soul

In the allegorical tradition of the Church Fathers, Abram represents both Christ and the faithful Christian soul, while Lot represents those who, though connected to the faith, choose according to carnal sight rather than spiritual vision. The separation of Abram and Lot thus prefigures the ultimate separation between those who walk by faith and those who walk by sight.

St. Irenaeus of Lyons, writing in Against Heresies, identifies Abram as a prophetic figure who foresaw Christ:

"Abraham was a prophet and saw in the Spirit the day of the Lord's coming, and the dispensation of His suffering, through whom both he himself and all who, following the example of his faith, trust in God, should be saved."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV

The return from Egypt to Canaan, with its movement from a land of bondage to the land of promise, allegorically represents the soul's journey from sin to grace, from worldly attachment to divine communion. Abram's return to the altar at Bethel ("House of God") signifies the restoration of the soul to its proper orientation toward God after periods of spiritual wandering.

The Two Ways: Faith and Sight

The contrast between Abram and Lot illustrates the fundamental biblical distinction between walking by faith and walking by sight. Lot "lifted up his eyes" and chose based on external appearances--the well-watered plain that resembled the paradise of the Lord. Abram, by contrast, waited upon God's direction and received a vision that encompassed far more than natural eyes could perceive.

This pattern is echoed throughout Scripture. As St. Paul writes: "For we walk by faith, not by sight" (2 Cor 5:7). Lot's choice represents the way of the flesh, which judges by appearances; Abram's way represents the path of faith, which trusts in God's promises even when circumstances seem unfavorable.

The Fathers saw in this narrative an allegory of the spiritual and carnal interpretations of Scripture itself. Origen, in his Homilies on Genesis, consistently distinguished between the literal ("carnal") and spiritual readings of the sacred text:

"The words of the Scripture are its body, or the visible element, that hides its spirit, or the invisible element."

Origen, De Principiis

Those who, like Lot, see only the surface beauty of Scripture miss its deeper spiritual meaning, while those who, like Abram, look beyond appearances discover the treasures hidden within.

The Jordan Plain and Worldly Allurements

The well-watered Jordan plain, described as "the paradise of the Lord" and compared to Egypt, represents the seductive beauty of worldly goods. What appears most attractive to natural sight often leads toward spiritual destruction. The text's ominous note that this description applied "before the Lord destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah" reveals that earthly paradises are subject to divine judgment.

Lot's choice to pitch his tent "even to Sodom" shows the gradual nature of spiritual compromise. He did not immediately enter Sodom; he dwelt near it. Yet proximity to sin leads inevitably to participation in sin. By Genesis 14, Lot is dwelling within Sodom itself, and by Genesis 19, he has become a resident whose family is thoroughly entangled with the doomed city.

The Promise of Innumerable Seed

The promise that Abram's seed would be "as the dust of the earth" has a twofold allegorical significance. First, it points to Christ, the singular "seed" through whom all the promises find their fulfillment, as St. Paul explains in Galatians 3:16. Second, it refers to the multitude of believers who become children of Abraham through faith.

Augustine teaches that Abraham is thus the father of two peoples--the physical Israel and the spiritual Israel of all nations:

"Two things are promised to Abraham, the one, that his seed should possess the land of Canaan... but the other far more excellent, not about the carnal but the spiritual seed, through which he is the father, not of the one Israelite nation, but of all nations who follow the footprints of his faith."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

Mamre and Hebron: Vision and Communion

Abram's settlement at Mamre in Hebron carries rich allegorical meaning. "Mamre" signifies "vision"--the spiritual sight that perceives divine realities beyond what natural eyes can see. "Hebron" means "communion" or "fellowship"--the intimate relationship with God that is the fruit of faith.

While Lot moved toward Sodom, pursuing the vision of his natural eyes, Abram moved toward a place whose very name means "vision"--not earthly vision, but the prophetic vision that perceives God's purposes. And while Lot would soon find himself in a city of strangers and sinners, Abram dwelt in "communion" with the Lord, building an altar for worship.

The Church and the Synagogue

Some patristic interpreters saw in Abram and Lot a typology of the Church and the Synagogue, or of spiritual and carnal Israel. Lot, though a kinsman of Abram and a participant in the promises, chose according to the flesh and suffered accordingly. This reading finds support in the later history, where Lot's descendants--Moab and Ammon--would become persistent adversaries of Israel, while Abram's descendants through Isaac and Jacob would inherit the covenant promises.
moral:
Moral (Tropological) Interpretation

The Virtue of Peacemaking

Genesis 13 presents Abram as a model peacemaker, embodying the beatitude: "Blessed are the peacemakers: for they shall be called the children of God" (Matt 5:9). Though he had every right to assert his priority as the elder and as the recipient of God's promise, Abram chose humility and conciliation over strife and self-assertion.

St. John Chrysostom, in his homilies, emphasizes the destructive nature of contentiousness and the strength that comes from concord:

"Nothing produces weakness so effectively as contentiousness and strife; and nothing produces power and strength so effectively as love and concord. When Solomon grasped this truth he said: 'A brother that is helped by his brother is like a strong city and kingdom bolted and barred.'"

St. John Chrysostom, Homilies

Abram's words, "Let there be no strife, I beseech thee, between me and thee... for we are brethren" (Gen 13:8), establish the foundation of Christian conflict resolution: the recognition of our common brotherhood under God takes precedence over material disputes. The strife was between the herdsmen, but Abram addresses Lot directly, taking responsibility for resolving the conflict rather than blaming servants or circumstances.

Humility and Generosity

Abram's offer to let Lot choose first demonstrates the virtue of humility united with generosity. He was willing to receive whatever portion remained after Lot's selection, trusting that God's providence would provide for him regardless of which land he occupied. This is a powerful lesson against grasping and possessiveness.

Augustine notes that Abram established a pattern for righteous conduct:

"From this, perhaps, has arisen a pacific custom among men, that when there is any partition of earthly things, the greater should make the division, the less the choice."

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI, Chapter 20

This principle--that those in positions of authority should be the first to sacrifice, not the first to claim--stands as a rebuke to worldly ambition. True spiritual leadership consists in serving others, not in securing advantages for oneself.

The Danger of Choosing by Appearances

Lot's choice provides a sobering moral lesson about the danger of judging by external appearances. The text emphasizes that Lot "lifted up his eyes" and made his decision based on what he saw--the well-watered plain, the fertile land, the apparent prosperity. He did not consult God, did not consider the moral character of his future neighbors, and did not weigh the spiritual consequences of his choice.

The Fathers consistently warned against this pattern of judgment. Lot's choice was rational by worldly standards but catastrophic by spiritual standards. He gained fertile land but lost his wife, nearly lost his daughters, and fathered children through incest who became enemies of God's people. The moral lesson is clear: what appears advantageous to carnal sight may lead to spiritual ruin.

St. Basil the Great, though writing about other passages, articulated the principle that applies here:

"I know the laws of allegory, though less by myself than from the works of others. There are those truly, who do not admit the common sense of the Scriptures... For me grass is grass; plant, fish, wild beast, domestic animal, I take all in the literal sense."

St. Basil the Great, Hexaemeron

Yet even Basil acknowledged that Scripture teaches us to look beyond surfaces. Lot saw grass--well-watered, abundant grass--and chose accordingly. Had he looked more deeply, he would have seen the wickedness of Sodom and fled in the opposite direction.

The Testimony Before Unbelievers

The mention that "the Canaanite and the Perizzite dwelled at that time in the land" (Gen 13:7) introduces an important moral consideration: the conduct of believers is witnessed by unbelievers. The strife between the herdsmen of Abram and Lot occurred before the watching eyes of pagan peoples. How this conflict was resolved would either commend or discredit the faith of these patriarchs.

This principle applies to the Church in every age. St. Paul writes: "Give none offense, neither to the Jews, nor to the Gentiles, nor to the church of God" (1 Cor 10:32). When Christians quarrel over material goods, they scandalize those outside the faith. When they resolve conflicts with charity and magnanimity, as Abram did, they bear witness to the transforming power of grace.

The Pattern of Worship

Abram's consistent practice of building altars and calling upon the name of the Lord provides a model for the spiritual life. At each significant location in his journey, Abram erected an altar--not merely as a memorial but as an act of worship and dedication. His life was marked by these sacred spaces where heaven and earth met.

The contrast with Lot is instructive. There is no record of Lot building altars or establishing places of worship. His movement toward Sodom was a movement away from the altars of his youth, away from the sacred spaces where God was honored. The moral lesson is that those who neglect worship gradually drift toward the world, while those who maintain regular communion with God remain anchored in faith.

Contentment and Trust in Providence

Abram's willingness to accept whatever land remained after Lot's choice demonstrates the virtue of contentment rooted in trust in divine providence. He knew that God's promises did not depend on his own striving or shrewd negotiations. The land God intended for him would be his, regardless of which portion Lot selected.

This is the disposition St. Paul commends: "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, to be content therewith" (Phil 4:11). The grasping, anxious pursuit of material security betrays a lack of faith in God's providential care. Abram's generous offer to Lot was an act of faith--a declaration that his security rested not in possession of land but in the promises of God.
anagogical:
Anagogical Interpretation

The Separation of the Righteous and the Wicked

The anagogical sense of Scripture interprets earthly realities as signs pointing to eternal glory and the final consummation of all things. The separation of Abram and Lot in Genesis 13 prefigures the ultimate separation that will occur at the Last Judgment, when Christ will divide humanity as a shepherd divides sheep from goats (Matt 25:31-46).

Abram and Lot represent two fundamental orientations of the human heart: toward God and toward the world. Their separation foreshadows the eternal separation between those who chose the narrow way that leads to life and those who chose the broad way that leads to destruction. Lot's movement toward Sodom--a city destined for divine judgment--anticipates the fate of all who set their hearts on earthly goods that will pass away.

Lot's Wife and the Danger of Looking Back

Though the account of Lot's wife turning to a pillar of salt occurs in Genesis 19, its seeds are planted here in Lot's choice to dwell near Sodom. St. Irenaeus of Lyons provides a profound eschatological interpretation of this figure:

"His wife remained in [the territory of] Sodore, no longer corruptible flesh, but a pillar of salt which endures for ever; and by those natural processes which appertain to the human race, indicating that the Church also, which is the salt of the earth, has been left behind within the confines of the earth, and subject to human sufferings."

St. Irenaeus, Against Heresies, Book IV, Chapter 31

Irenaeus interprets the pillar of salt as a type of the Church, which remains as "salt of the earth" within the boundaries of this world, preserving it from complete corruption while enduring the sufferings of earthly existence. The salt pillar represents "the foundation of the faith which makes strong, and sends forward, children to their Father."

The Land of Promise and the Heavenly Country

The land promised to Abram--extending in all directions from where he stood--is a type of the heavenly inheritance that awaits the faithful. When God commanded Abram to "lift up thy eyes" and survey the land, He was inviting him to see by faith what could not yet be possessed in fact. This is the pattern of Christian hope: we see the heavenly country from afar and live as pilgrims moving toward it.

The Letter to the Hebrews makes this connection explicit, describing the patriarchs as those who "confessed that they are pilgrims and strangers on the earth" and who "seek a country... a better, that is to say, a heavenly country" (Heb 11:13-16). The earthly Canaan was but a shadow and foretaste of the true promised land that awaits the people of God.

Seed as the Dust of the Earth: The Resurrection

The promise that Abram's seed would be "as the dust of the earth" contains a hidden eschatological meaning. Dust is associated in Scripture with mortality and death--"dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return" (Gen 3:19). Yet from this dust of death, God raises up innumerable children for Abraham.

This points toward the resurrection of the dead, when the mortal puts on immortality and the corruptible puts on incorruption. The countless grains of dust, individually insignificant but collectively beyond numbering, represent the vast multitude that will be raised on the last day--the communion of saints drawn from every nation, tribe, and tongue.

Augustine addresses the scope of this promise:

"For who does not see how incomparably larger the number of the dust must be than all men from Adam to the end of the world? How much greater must it be than the seed of Abraham--not only that pertaining to the nation of Israel, but also that which is and shall be according to the imitation of faith in all nations of the whole wide world!"

St. Augustine, City of God, Book XVI

Mamre and the Vision of God

Abram's settlement at Mamre ("vision") in Hebron ("communion") points toward the beatific vision that constitutes the eternal life of the blessed. In this life, we see "through a glass, darkly; but then face to face" (1 Cor 13:12). The faithful, like Abram, journey toward that place of perfect vision and unbroken communion with God.

It is significant that at Mamre, Abram would later receive the visitation of three angelic visitors (Gen 18), traditionally understood as a Trinitarian theophany. The place of "vision" became a place where God was seen. This anticipates heaven itself, where the pure in heart will see God (Matt 5:8) and where there will be no temple, "for the Lord God Almighty is the temple thereof, and the Lamb" (Rev 21:22).

The Judgment of Sodom and the Final Judgment

The brief but ominous description of Sodom's inhabitants as "very wicked, and sinners before the face of the Lord beyond measure" (Gen 13:13) foreshadows both their temporal destruction and the final judgment that awaits all who persist in wickedness. Christ Himself used Sodom as a type of judgment, warning that it would be more tolerable for Sodom on the day of judgment than for cities that rejected His apostles (Matt 10:15).

The destruction of Sodom by fire and brimstone (Gen 19) became in Christian tradition a type of the final conflagration that will consume the present heavens and earth (2 Pet 3:7). Yet just as Lot was rescued from Sodom before its destruction, so the righteous will be delivered before the day of wrath. The anagogical reading thus holds together both warning and hope: judgment is coming, but salvation is available to all who, like Abram, walk by faith and not by sight.

The Altar and the Heavenly Liturgy

Abram's altar at Mamre points toward the eternal liturgy of heaven, where the worship that begins on earth reaches its perfection. Every earthly altar is a participation in and anticipation of the heavenly altar described in Revelation, where the Lamb who was slain receives the worship of angels and saints.

The faithful who, like Abram, build altars of devotion in their earthly pilgrimage are preparing for that eternal worship. The temporary altars of stone give way to the permanent altar of the heavenly Jerusalem, and the prayers offered in time join the unceasing hymn of eternity: "Blessing, and glory, and wisdom, and thanksgiving, and honour, and power, and strength to our God for ever and ever" (Rev 7:12).
